name: Shecyü, a Tangshang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xiii+225 pp. (open PDF, the Internet Archive the Internet Archive 2018 capture of the Payap linguistics-students repository)

catalog_quote: The minor syllables in sesquisyllabic words have no contrastive tone. Pitch is always mid, [T³]. However, there is contrastive tone in the syllabic bilabial nasal /m̩/ for some grammatical morphemes, as shown for instance in (6). ... There is a high-falling tone harmony process with a single word shown in (7) where the second syllable is originally with a mid-level-tone /ɲe²/. ... Shecyü has no stress. The author has observed occasional idiolectal tonal free-variation for some speakers in Chamchang, a Shecyü dialect found in India.

The author has observed occasional…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shecyü (a Pangwa Tangsa variety) is a three-tone language (high-falling, mid-level, mid-falling on unchecked syllables; checked syllables non-contrastive) and the author states flatly that it has no stress. Word prosody is carried by tone; sesquisyllabic words have a toneless minor (schwa) syllable followed by a tone-bearing major syllable. Morey 2014 (LD&C 8: 661-662, Mueshaungx and Chamchang) adds the phonetic side: these languages are iambic, the first syllable of a disyllable is 'reduced and less stressed' (shorter, less intensity, reduced pitch fall), the second syllable is the prominent one.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Tone: minor syllables of sesquisyllables are toneless (always mid pitch); syllabic nasal /m̩/ can carry contrastive tone; a high-tone harmony process within words (p. 44); Mungre likewise has toneless minor syllables (p. 65) but no stress statement is made for Mungre.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on elicited wordlist/citation forms (about 2,400 items per variety) plus recordings; Morey 2014's iambic/reduced-first-syllable observation concerns disyllabic words in citation form (kufkuf 'dog', wushawx 'bird').
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 tase1235 covers the Pangwa Tangsa dialects (Cholim tong1312, Muishaung mosa1240, Mungre mung1264, Chamchang kims1240, Shecyu-Chamchang shec1234, Rera-Hajang rera1241, Joglei, Ngaimong, Hahcheng, Longri, Lochhang, Maitai, etc.). The quoted statement is about Shecyü (Myanmar; Chamchang is its Indian dialect) = shec1234/kims1240 under tase1235; Khan 2017 also covers Mungre (mung1264). The two sources the earlier scan named are OUTSIDE tase1235 in Glottolog: Boro 2017 Hakhun = hakh1236 (under Nocte Naga noct1238) and Mulder 2020 Muklom = mukl1235 (Muklomic mukl1234). Morey 2014 pp. 661-662 (Mueshaungx = mosa1240, Chamchang = kims1240) supports the reading for other Pangwa varieties.

tone_statements.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker. 2025. On the independence of tonogenesis in Patkaian branches. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 48(2): 163-192. doi:10.1075/ltba.25011.dam
tone_statements.quote: The tone system found in the northern branch of Patkaian, also known as Tangsa-Nocte8 is fundamentally a 4-toneme system with surface similarities to that of Middle Chinese, or to the 4-way split of Tai tones9 into A B C and D, where one category is “checked” or “dead”. Across dozens of varieties, the tonemes are cognate … Tone 1 is a reflex of creaky phonation … Tone 2 in Tangsa-Nocte derives from words with modal phonation in the proto language, and is by far the most frequently occurring toneme. … Fourth tone is found only on CVC syllables, and functions as its own toneme
tone_statements.locator: p. 170, §2.1 'Tangsa-Nocte-Tutsa-Ollo (Northern branch)'; Table 2 'Tones in Muishaung Tangsa' p. 171
tone_statements.summary: Four tonemes in Tangsa-Nocte: tones 1-3 on non-checked syllables (Muishaung values 31, 231, 333) plus checked tone 4 on stop-final syllables; low functional load; some varieties merge to three.

tone_statements.quote: A complete wordlist is unavailable, and the examples given by Coupe do appear to offer only a broad phonetic transcription of tone, with most words typically marked simply as 11:, 33: or 55:. There is not a clear explanation as to the differing transcriptions of the pitch values. [...] It may be the case that there is indeed a correspondence between tone categories for Chang and Tangsa-Nocte, at least to the extent that such exists between Tangsa-Nocte and Phong. Further investigation is needed on this subject.
tone_statements.summary: Secondhand: three Chang tonemes 55 / 51 / 11 (Coupe), with [33] allotone of 55 before 11; no tonal correspondence with Tangsa-Nocte categories established.

tone_statements.quote: The toneme system of Tangsa (Jugli dialect) is represen- table in terms of a three-toneme pitch tone system, with /1/ = low, /°/ = mid, 7/ = high. Two peculiarities exist: Tone /1/ syllables are obligatorily pronounced with a glottal stop if the syllable is in isolated or final position … and there are syllables with very short vowels in pitch /2/ and final glottal stop which is never elided (such that we consider the glottal stop as primary and omit the pitch sign in redundancy- free phonemic representations).
tone_statements.locator: p. 85, sec. 4 'Evidence for claim 2'; Diagram 2 on p. 86; verb alternations sec. 5 pp. 107-111
tone_statements.summary: Jugli Tangsa: three level tonemes, /1/ low, /2/ mid, /3/ high; final low-tone syllables end in a redundant glottal stop; checked /CVʔ/ syllables take no tone sign; verb stems alternate in tone.

sources.note: §2.5 Stress, p. 63: 'Stress is not contrastive in Hakhun, most probably because one of the correlates of stress, namely pitch, is used for lexical contrast.
